title: Data, analytics and reading data carefully
summary: Spurious correlation (shark attacks and ice-cream), the attrition story, the role of analytics, course outcomes and reading two class-performance graphs.

chunks.heading: Shark attacks and ice-cream sales
chunks.explanation_md:
The chart on the slide shows **shark attacks** and **ice-cream sales** month by month. Both are low in Jan, climb through May, **peak together in July**, and fall again by Nov.

Does ice-cream cause shark attacks? No. The next slide shows the real story: **summer** drives both. In summer more people buy ice-cream and more people swim in the sea.

This is called a **spurious correlation**: two things move together, but neither causes the other. The slide points to tylervigen.com for many such examples.

key_terms.meaning: Two things that move together without one causing the other, because something else (here, summer) drives both.

chunks.exam_line: Shark attacks and ice-cream sales rise together because summer drives both: a spurious correlation, not cause and effect.

clarification.text: A relationship in data that looks meaningful but happens only because a third factor affects both things.

chunks.heading: The employee attrition story
chunks.explanation_md:
A company with a healthy, thriving culture in a scenic setting had **alarming levels of attrition**. HR and fellow employees noticed it. HR gave a **statistician** the data for all employees; she fed it into a model and came up with numbers and charts.

Her conclusion: **employees below the age of 30 who live 20+ miles from work do not stay for long.**

The story shows how data turns a vague worry ("people keep leaving") into a specific, testable pattern that a manager can act on.

chunks.heading: The role of analytics in modern management
chunks.explanation_md:
**Everyday decisions increasingly rely on data.** Businesses collect massive amounts of it: sales, customer behaviour, operations. **Analytics transforms data into actionable insights**, and **data visualisation and dashboards** matter because they make those insights easy to see.

Example: a **restaurant chain** analyzes customer visit data to identify **peak business hours and plan staffing**.

The course aims to build skills in statistical analysis and inference, probability and risk assessment, forecasting and optimisation, interpreting business data, and **decision-making based on evidence, not gut feeling**. Quantitative techniques help managers make **informed, objective and defensible decisions** and navigate uncertainty.

The module also recommends two videos: *Are athletes really getting faster, better, stronger?* and *Hans Rosling's 200 Countries, 200 Years, 4 Minutes*.
chunks.exam_line: Analytics transforms data into actionable insights; quantitative techniques help managers make informed, objective and defensible decisions based on evidence, not gut feeling.

chunks.heading: Reading two class-performance graphs
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide asks: **how do you interpret Graph A and Graph B in terms of class performance?**

- **Graph A (AIM):** the curve **peaks towards the right** and has a **long tail stretching to the left**.
- **Graph B (QTM):** the curve **peaks towards the left** and has a **long tail stretching to the right**.

Reading them as distributions of marks: in Graph A most of the class is bunched at the higher end with a few low scores trailing behind; in Graph B most of the class is bunched at the lower end with a few high scores trailing ahead. The position of the peak and the direction of the tail describe the **shape** of the data, one of the measures of descriptive statistics.
chunks.exam_line: Graph A (AIM) peaks to the right with a long left tail; Graph B (QTM) peaks to the left with a long right tail: the shape of a distribution tells you where most of the class scored.

questions.stem: What is a spurious correlation? Explain it using the shark attack and ice-cream sales chart.
questions.model_answer_md:
Two things can move together without one causing the other.

- **The chart:** shark attacks and ice-cream sales are both low in Jan, climb through May, **peak together in July** and fall again by Nov.
- **The trap:** it is tempting to say ice-cream causes shark attacks, or the other way round.
- **The real driver:** the next slide puts **summer** in the middle. In summer more people buy ice-cream and more people swim, so both lines rise.
- **Spurious correlation:** two variables move together, but **neither causes the other**; a third factor drives both.

So a manager must ask what really drives a pattern before acting on it.

Summer is the common driver of both
Spurious correlation: variables move together without a causal link

questions.stem: Differentiate between sample statistics and population parameters, as defined in Module 1.
questions.model_answer_md:
The same measures get different names depending on whose data they come from.

| Basis | Sample statistic | Population parameter |
|---|---|---|
| **Computed from** | Data from a **sample** | Data from the whole **population** |
| **Role** | The **point estimator** of the matching parameter | The value being estimated |

The measures themselves are the same kinds: **central tendency, variation/dispersion and shape**.

So a sample statistic is our best single estimate of the population parameter.

rubric.point: Measures from sample data are sample statistics
Measures from population data are population parameters
A sample statistic is the point estimator of the population parameter

questions.stem: Differentiate between Graph A (AIM) and Graph B (QTM) on the class performance slide. What does each tell you about the class, and which descriptive measure describes the difference?
questions.model_answer_md:
The slide asks how to interpret two graphs of marks in terms of class performance. Both are distributions, but they lean opposite ways.

| Basis | Graph A (AIM) | Graph B (QTM) |
|---|---|---|
| **Peak** | Towards the **right** | Towards the **left** |
| **Long tail** | Stretches to the **left** | Stretches to the **right** |
| **Most students** | Bunched at the **higher end** of marks | Bunched at the **lower end** of marks |
| **The few** | A few **low scores** trail behind | A few **high scores** trail ahead |

**Reading Graph A (AIM):** most of the class did well; only a handful of students scored low. Class performance is strong overall.

**Reading Graph B (QTM):** most of the class scored low; only a handful of students reached high marks. Most students found this subject harder.

**Which measure:** descriptive statistics uses three kinds of measures: **central tendency**, **variation/dispersion** and **shape**. The position of the peak and the direction of the tail describe the **shape** of the data. Two classes could even share an average and still have these opposite shapes, so looking at the whole picture matters.

**Conclusion:** Graph A shows a mostly high-scoring class with a few weak scores; Graph B shows a mostly low-scoring class with a few strong scores, and the difference is one of shape.

rubric.point: Graph A peaks right with a long left tail
Graph B peaks left with a long right tail
AIM: most students scored high, few low
QTM: most students scored low, few high
Peak and tail describe the shape of the data
Three kinds of measures: central tendency, dispersion, shape

questions.stem: "Data must be read carefully before managers act on it." Discuss this statement using the shark attack chart, the employee attrition story and the role of analytics described in Module 1.
questions.model_answer_md:
Module 1 shows that data is powerful, but only when it is read with care.

**1. Patterns can mislead (shark attacks and ice-cream).**
- The chart shows **shark attacks** and **ice-cream sales** low in Jan, rising through May, **peaking together in July** and falling by Nov.
- It looks as if one causes the other, but the next slide shows **summer** drives both: more people buy ice-cream and more people swim.
- This is a **spurious correlation**. Acting on it (say, cutting ice-cream sales to stop shark attacks) would be a mistake.

**2. Data can reveal a real, usable pattern (employee attrition).**
- A company with a healthy culture had **alarming attrition**. HR gave a **statistician** data for **all employees**.
- Her model found that **employees below the age of 30 who live 20+ miles from work do not stay for long**.
- A vague worry became a **specific, testable pattern** HR can act on.

**3. Analytics as a management tool.**
- **Everyday decisions increasingly rely on data**; firms collect massive data on sales, customer behaviour and operations.
- **Analytics transforms data into actionable insights**, and **visualisation and dashboards** help people see them.
- Example: a **restaurant chain** uses customer visit data to find **peak hours and plan staffing**.

**4. Why care matters.** The course aims at **decision-making based on evidence, not gut feeling**, so decisions are **informed, objective and defensible**. Evidence read carelessly is no better than a guess.

**Conclusion:** the shark chart warns that moving together is not cause; the attrition story and the restaurant example show what careful analysis can deliver.
